client: I've been really struggling lately with everything piling up at work. My boss just dumped two new projects on me with these insane deadlines, and I'm already stretched thin at the marketing agency. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, because the work is still going to be there when I walk out of here.
therapist: It sounds like you're carrying a real weight right now, and I appreciate you being honest about your skepticism — that's actually a really important thing to name. You're right that the workload will still be there, and I don't want to pretend otherwise; what we can explore together is how your *relationship* with that pressure might shift, which can make a genuine difference in how you move through it. What do you think is the hardest part for you right now — the volume of work itself, or something about how you're thinking and feeling about it?

client: Honestly, I think it's more about how I'm feeling about it than the actual amount of work, but that almost makes it worse somehow — like I should be able to just handle it and the fact that I can't means something is wrong with me. There's this constant background noise of anxiety telling me I'm falling behind, even on days when I'm technically keeping up. And then I feel guilty for not being more grateful or productive, which just adds another layer on top of everything.
therapist: What you just described — that loop of anxiety, then guilt for feeling anxious, then more pressure — is really exhausting to live with, even when things are technically "okay" on the outside. I want to gently challenge that thought that struggling means something is *wrong* with you, because what you're actually describing sounds like a very human response to sustained pressure, not a personal failing. Can you tell me more about where that belief comes from — the idea that you *should* just be able to handle it?

client: I think it comes from my family, honestly. Growing up, there was this unspoken rule that you just pushed through things and didn't complain, and if you struggled it meant you weren't trying hard enough. So now whenever I feel anxious at work or overwhelmed, there's this voice in my head that sounds a lot like my dad saying "just get on with it."
therapist: It takes real self-awareness to trace that voice back to its source, and it sounds like you've carried your dad's message for a long time — so long that it probably feels like *your* voice now, even though it was handed to you before you had any say in the matter. In CBT we'd call that a core belief, and the important thing is that beliefs we inherited aren't the same as facts, even when they feel absolutely true. I'm curious — if a close friend came to you feeling exactly the way you've been feeling at work, would you tell them to "just get on with it"?

client: Honestly, no, I wouldn't say that to a friend. I'd probably tell them it makes sense they're struggling and that they should be kinder to themselves. But somehow when it's me, that same logic just... doesn't land the same way, and I don't really know why.
therapist: That gap you just noticed — being able to offer compassion to a friend but not to yourself — is actually one of the most common and important things we work with in therapy, and the fact that you can see it so clearly is a real strength. The reason it doesn't "land" for you is likely because that inner critic has had decades of practice, while self-compassion is still a newer, quieter voice that hasn't built up the same muscle yet. What do you think it would feel like, even just for a moment, to try speaking to yourself the way you'd speak to that friend?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to try it, but honestly it feels kind of... hollow when I attempt it. Like I can picture saying "hey, you made a mistake, it's okay, you're still a good person" to myself, but it just sounds fake in my own head, like I'm lying to myself. The critic feels true, and the kind voice feels like I'm just making excuses.
therapist: That feeling of hollowness is really common and actually makes a lot of sense — the critic feels true because it's been reinforced thousands of times, while the kind voice is so new it doesn't have any evidence behind it yet, so of course it feels unconvincing. The goal isn't to force yourself to *believe* the kind voice right away, but to start gently questioning whether the critic is actually as accurate as it feels — because "feeling true" and "being true" aren't the same thing. So I'm wondering, can you think of a specific recent moment where the critic told you that you were falling short — and we could look together at what the actual evidence for and against that thought really was?

client: I guess... there was this moment last week where I didn't reach out to a friend who I knew was going through something hard. The critic was really loud about that — like, "you're selfish, you're a bad friend, you only think about yourself." And honestly, sitting here right now, it still feels pretty true, because I did know she was struggling and I just... didn't do anything.
therapist: That moment is clearly still sitting heavily with you, and I want to make sure we look at it carefully rather than just accepting the critic's verdict. So let's gently examine the evidence — the critic says "you only think about yourself," but you're sitting here *right now* feeling genuine pain about your friend's wellbeing, which doesn't really sound like someone who only thinks about themselves. What was actually going on for you that week when you didn't reach out — was there anything else weighing on you that might have made it harder to show up?

client: I mean... yeah, that week was actually really bad for me too. I was barely sleeping, I had that work deadline that felt like it was going to swallow me whole, and honestly I was kind of in survival mode just getting through each day. But I still feel like that's just an excuse, like I should have found a way to check in on her no matter what was going on with me.
therapist: What you just described — barely sleeping, drowning in a deadline, in pure survival mode — isn't an "excuse," it's *context*, and there's a really meaningful difference between those two things. The belief that you should be able to show up perfectly for others regardless of what's happening to you is actually the same impossible standard your dad's voice installed, just wearing a different mask. I'm curious — do you think you'd call it "just an excuse" if your friend told you *she* hadn't reached out to *you* during a week like that?

client: I mean... no, obviously I wouldn't call it an excuse if she did that. I'd probably tell her I completely understood and that she should have just focused on herself. But it feels different when it's me — like there's this double standard I can't seem to turn off, and I know that even as I'm saying it out loud.
therapist: The fact that you can name that double standard out loud, in real time, is genuinely significant — that's not a small thing, because most people live inside that pattern for years without ever seeing it so clearly. What you're describing is essentially a rule that says "everyone deserves understanding and grace *except* me," and it's worth asking where you learned that your struggles count for less than everyone else's. Do you think that belief — that others deserve compassion but you somehow don't — shows up in other areas of your life beyond friendship?

client: Yeah, it shows up everywhere, honestly. Like at work, if I make a mistake I'll replay it for days, but if a colleague messes up I just think "oh, they probably had a lot going on." I never extend that same logic to myself — it's like I'm operating under a completely different set of rules and I don't even question it until you point it out like that.
therapist: What you're describing is a really significant pattern — two completely different rulebooks, one generous and flexible for everyone else, and one harsh and unforgiving reserved just for you, and it's been running so quietly in the background that it never got questioned. This is actually the heart of a lot of what we'd work on together — not trying to lower your standards, but bringing the standards you naturally apply to others into your own life too, so you're playing by one fair set of rules instead of two. I'm wondering, now that you're starting to see this pattern more clearly, does any part of you feel ready to gently experiment with catching that double standard in the moment — and what do you think that might look like for you?

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me does recognize that double standard when you lay it out like that. But honestly, when I'm in the middle of it — like when I've made a mistake at work or let someone down — it doesn't feel like a double standard, it just feels like the truth about me. I'm not sure I'd even be able to catch it in the moment because it feels so real and justified when it's happening.
therapist: What you're describing is actually one of the trickiest things about deeply held beliefs — they don't announce themselves as beliefs, they just feel like reality, which is exactly what makes them so hard to catch in the moment. So rather than expecting yourself to challenge the thought while you're in the flood of it, we could work on building that awareness *after* the fact first — like a kind of gentle detective work where you look back at moments like the ones you've described and practice spotting the double standard with a bit more distance. Over time, that "noticing muscle" tends to get stronger and starts to work faster — but I'm curious, is there a small, low-stakes moment from your week where we could try practicing that together right now?
